lead: A set of premises is consistent when one single truth assignment makes all of them true together; if no such assignment exists, the set is inconsistent. The CP rule, short for conditional proof, proves P → Q by assuming P for a while, deriving Q, then discharging that assumption. Consistency checks catch a contradictory specification before money is spent on it. Only a few universities teach this material.
prereq: You need 1.4 for modus ponens and 1.1 for truth tables.

blocks.text: A truth assignment gives every propositional variable the value T (true) or F (false). A set of premises S = {P₁, P₂, …, Pₙ} is consistent when one assignment makes every Pᵢ true at the same time. If no assignment does that, S is inconsistent.
Consistency belongs to the whole set, not to one formula. Taken alone, p → q and p are each satisfiable, yet {p → q, p, ¬q} is inconsistent.

items: Count the distinct variables, n; the truth table has 2ⁿ rows.
Fill T or F for each premise in every row.
One row with all premises T means consistent; no such row means inconsistent.

blocks.text: A second test is derivation. Apply the rules of inference from 1.4. If two lines give Q and ¬Q, the set is inconsistent. For {p → q, q → r, p, ¬r}: p with p → q gives q, then q with q → r gives r, which clashes with ¬r.
The CP rule proves an implication P → Q without building a truth table. Assume P, derive Q, then close the assumption and write P → Q.

items: Write “Assume P — CP” and mark the line as temporary.
Derive Q using the premises and the rules of inference.
Discharge P: write P → Q, citing the assumption line and the line where Q appeared.
Lines inside the sub-proof stay shut after discharge, except through the new implication.

blocks.text: The assumption is not a premise of the theorem. p → r is proved from p → q and q → r alone; p was borrowed and returned.
CP nests. For P → (Q → R): assume P, assume Q, derive R, discharge Q to get Q → R, then discharge P. Discharge in the reverse order of assumption.

An argument with premises Γ and conclusion C is valid exactly when Γ ∪ {¬C} is inconsistent. To prove C, add ¬C as a temporary assumption and derive a contradiction; ¬C must then be false, so C holds.

items: Negate the conclusion C and add ¬C to the premises.
Derive some formula and its negation.
Reject ¬C, conclude C, and drop ¬C from the premise list.

blocks.text: This is the indirect proof of 1.7 in propositional form. CP and this method say the same thing: assuming P and reaching Q is finding P ∧ ¬Q impossible.

figure.caption: The temporary assumption p yields q and r by two uses of modus ponens; the last step discharges p and gives p → r.

spec.title: CP proof of p→r
spec.aria: A conditional-proof flow: assume p, derive q and r, then discharge p to conclude p→r.

examples.question: Prove p → r from the premises p → q and q → r using the CP rule. Then decide whether the four formulas p → q, q → r, p, ¬r are consistent.
steps: Line 1: p → q, premise. Line 2: q → r, premise.
Line 3: assume p, CP start, marked temporary.
Line 4: q, by modus ponens on line 1 (p → q) and line 3 (p).
Line 5: r, by modus ponens on line 2 (q → r) and line 4 (q).
Line 6: discharge p and write p → r by CP, citing lines 3 to 5.
Consistency test: p with p → q gives q; q with q → r gives r; r clashes with ¬r. A truth table over 3 variables has 8 rows, and 0 rows make all four premises true.
examples.answer: p → r is proved by CP, and the premises p → q, q → r, p, ¬r are inconsistent: 0 of 8 rows satisfy all four.
examples.check:
from itertools import product

premises = [
    lambda p, q, r: (not p) or q,
    lambda p, q, r: (not q) or r,
    lambda p, q, r: p,
    lambda p, q, r: not r,
]

rows = list(product([True, False], repeat=3))
sat = [v for v in rows if all(f(*v) for f in premises)]
print(len(sat))
print(len(rows))

traps: The CP assumption is temporary: discharge it before the final line and never list it as a premise.
Rows are 2ⁿ for n variables, not 2n.
A valid argument may have inconsistent premises; anything then follows from them.
Discharge the very formula you assumed: the CP line must be P → Q with that same P.
Consistency is checked row by row for the whole set, not formula by formula.

quiz.q: Define a consistent set of premises.
quiz.a: A set S is consistent when at least one truth assignment makes every formula in S true at the same time; otherwise S is inconsistent.
p with p → q forces q by modus ponens; q and ¬q cannot both be true, so no assignment satisfies all three.

quiz.q: Is {p ∨ q, ¬p, ¬q} consistent? Show the reasoning.
quiz.a: Inconsistent. ¬p forces p = F and ¬q forces q = F, so p ∨ q is F; no row satisfies all three.

quiz.q: Use CP to prove (p ∧ q) → p.
quiz.a: Assume p ∧ q on a temporary line; simplification gives p; discharge the assumption and write (p ∧ q) → p.

quiz.q: If Γ is inconsistent, what can you say about Γ ⊢ C for any formula C?
quiz.a: It is valid for every C, because no assignment makes Γ true, so none makes Γ true and C false at once.

quiz.q: How does a CP assumption differ from a premise?
quiz.a: A premise holds for the whole proof; a CP assumption holds only inside its sub-proof and is removed when the implication is written.

beyond: Not for the exam. Consistency checking is what SAT and SMT solvers do, inside hardware equivalence checking, planning and program verification. The CP rule is the implication-introduction step of natural deduction, the logic that proof assistants such as Coq and Lean are built on. Search “SAT solver”, “SMT solver” and “natural deduction implication introduction” next.
